questions.q: What does parse_dates=["order_date"] do in pd.read_csv()?
options: Sorts the DataFrame by that column automatically
Converts that column to a real datetime64 type while reading the file, instead of leaving it as plain text
questions.explain: Without parse_dates, order_date loads as a plain object/string column, which doesn't support reliable date comparisons.

questions.q: After loading orders.csv with parse_dates=["order_date"], how many orders have an order_date on or after 2026-01-10?
questions.explain: Orders 1009 through 1020 (12 rows) fall on or after 2026-01-10.

questions.q: What default JSON shape does pd.read_json() expect to load as a DataFrame?
options: A JSON array where each element is one record/row represented as an object
An Excel file saved with a .json extension
A single nested object with no arrays
A plain string of comma-separated values
questions.explain: That's exactly the shape json.dump(orders, f) produced in Lesson 15 — a list of row-dicts.

questions.q: What does pd.read_excel() require that pd.read_csv() and pd.read_json() do not?
options: The openpyxl package installed, to read modern .xlsx files
questions.explain: read_csv and read_json only need pandas itself; read_excel needs openpyxl (or a similar engine) for .xlsx files.

questions.q: What does the sheet_name parameter of pd.read_excel() control?
options: Which worksheet within the Excel file gets loaded, by name or index
Whether the file is read as CSV instead of Excel
questions.explain: Leaving sheet_name off loads the first sheet by default; it can also be set to a specific name or index.
